plan.summary: The span-timing test in the tea package fakes a clock that starts at 1000 ms and passes those numbers to OpenTelemetry as span start and end times. The OpenTelemetry trace SDK (sdk-trace-base 2.x) handles a plain number that is no larger than `performance.now()` as a time measured from process start, and shifts it to wall-clock time. So once the test worker has been up for more than about a second, which happens under the full `pnpm test` run, the root span no longer starts at [1, 0] and the start and end times can come from different time bases. Run alone, the worker is new and the numbers are read as epoch milliseconds. The fix: traced span times always mean exactly the milliseconds the run reported, however long the process has been up. Then the test passes the same way in the full suite and alone.

The test-only fix hides that. The second and third criteria only apply with the library fix. With a test-only fix, they would be dropped and only the first would stay.

plan.summary: Today `code-graph --boundaries` skips every import whose importer is outside all declared features and outside `lib`. So with one feature declared, the rest of the codebase can import that feature's internals and `--boundaries --ci` stays green. The current test suite even asserts this ("leaves a file outside every feature and lib unjudged"). 504.name: ask:owner:questions

plan.summary: Today a `--layer-rules` path pattern can only be a directory prefix, with `*` allowed only as a whole segment. `**` and a `*` inside a filename are read as literal text, so a layer like `**/*-plumbing.ts` claims nothing and every edge is counted unlayered. After the fix, `**` matches any number of folders (including none) and `*` inside a segment matches part of a name without crossing a `/`. Plain prefixes keep working as they do now. When patterns overlap, a pattern with more literal text wins, and a tie between two layers is refused instead of being settled silently by alphabetical order.

Current order is depth, then literal-segment count, then alphabetical by pattern. Under depth-first, `**/*-plumbing.ts` (2 segments) loses to `services/*/src/domain` (4). The last fallback is alphabetical, which is the silent tie the ticket wants refused.
Already refuses duplicate layer names and the same pattern in two layers, and reports through `Reporter`, which gives exit 2. This is the natural home for the tie refusal.
`paths` is a plain string array. A pattern with an invalid shape (e.g. `a**b`) could be rejected here if wanted.

questions.ask: When a directory-prefix layer and a filename-role layer both claim a file, which one wins?
options: Most literal characters wins (count only the non-wildcard text), with segment count as a later tie-break
Keep depth first, then literal characters (a deep directory prefix beats `**/*-role.ts`)
Any pattern with a filename part always beats a pure directory prefix
questions.why: The ticket asks for this to be predictable but does not pick a winner, and users will notice the result. Counting literal characters ranks `apps/web/**/*-x.ts` above `**/*-x.ts` and does not punish `**` for being short. Keeping depth first would let almost any directory layer override a filename role. The two criteria about a directory layer and a role layer claiming the same file depend on this.

questions.ask: How is a specificity tie between different layers refused: only when the two patterns can actually claim the same file, or whenever their scores are equal?
options: Refuse only when the tied patterns overlap (checked by analysing the patterns when the rules file is resolved)
Refuse at run time when a scanned file is actually matched by two tied patterns
Refuse any tie in score, overlapping or not
questions.lean: Refuse only when the tied patterns overlap, checked when the rules file is resolved
questions.why: Refusing every tie would break ordinary configs like `apps/api` and `apps/web` in different layers, which score the same but never collide. Checking when the file is resolved matches the ticket's 'at the schema boundary', but it needs an overlap test between two patterns. Refusing at run time is simpler, but whether it fires depends on which files exist. The two tie criteria depend on this.
